distillation_scope: Pure disease-name first-layer leaf distillation for Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome. Cold-triggered, childhood, adult, intermittent, continuous, neurologic, ocular, audiologic, articular, amyloid, and severe neonatal-spectrum presentations are represented as mechanisms, axes, risk factors, event hazards, and context rather than as disease-name qualifiers.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Constitutive or low-threshold cryopyrin/NLRP3 inflammasome activation creates the inherited or de novo substrate for CAPS across its severity spectrum.
NLRP3 activation increases caspase-1-dependent IL-1 beta signaling, driving fever, acute-phase markers, neutrophilia, fatigue, pain, and organ inflammation.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Triggered or spontaneous inflammatory flare gate
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Cold exposure, stress, infection, vaccination, exercise, or no identifiable trigger can gate recurrent attacks, while severe disease may remain continuously active.
Innate neutrophilic inflammation produces urticaria-like nonpruritic rash, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, anemia of inflammation, and elevated CRP/SAA/ESR.
IL-1-driven ocular and meningeal inflammation causes conjunctivitis, uveitis, headache, papilledema, raised intracranial pressure, chronic aseptic meningitis, seizures, and visual-risk events.
Chronic inner-ear inflammation produces progressive high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss and can become irreversible when treatment is delayed.
Synovial, periarticular, and growth-plate inflammation causes arthralgia, arthritis, patellar/knee overgrowth, bony swelling, clubbing, frontal bossing, growth failure, and disability.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: SAA-driven AA amyloid and renal organ damage
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Persistent serum amyloid A elevation from uncontrolled inflammation can cause AA amyloidosis, proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, kidney failure, and downstream mortality risk.

axes.clinical_meaning: History of recurrent or persistent sterile systemic inflammatory episodes with fever, rash, pain, or organ inflammation.
Continuous inflammatory activity between attacks, more common in severe disease but not required.
Inflammatory episodes that reliably follow external or physiologic triggers such as cold exposure, stress, infection, vaccination, or exercise.
Duration of individual inflammatory episodes, ranging from hours to days or longer depending on activity pattern.
Frequency of recognizable febrile or inflammatory attacks.
General rash burden; CAPS usually expresses a recurrent urticaria-like or polymorphic neutrophilic rash.
Evanescent urticaria-like, maculopapular, or wheal-like neutrophilic eruption typical of CAPS.
Migratory, non-itchy, evanescent pattern that separates CAPS rash from ordinary histamine-mediated urticaria.
Tender pretibial nodular panniculitis; uncommon but reported with CAPS and should not define the leaf.
Measured fever during attacks or continuous inflammation.
History of fever even if a single snapshot is afebrile.
Composite activity when literature reports elevated CRP, SAA, ESR, neutrophilia, or thrombocytosis without exact values.
CRP commonly rises with IL-1-driven inflammation and normalizes with effective IL-1 blockade.
SAA is a sensitive inflammation marker and the substrate for AA amyloidosis risk.
ESR often rises with active CAPS but may be less synchronized than CRP or SAA.
Leukocytosis can be marked in active CAPS and may mimic infection.
Neutrophilia reflects innate inflammatory activation.
Reactive thrombocytosis may accompany chronic or severe inflammation.
Anemia of inflammation, iron deficiency from chronic disease context, or severe chronic illness can lower hemoglobin.
Conjunctival inflammation or congestion during CAPS activity.
Inflammatory uveitis as part of ocular CAPS involvement.
Optic-disc swelling from chronic intracranial or ocular inflammatory involvement.
Headache from systemic inflammation, aseptic meningitis, or raised intracranial pressure.
Sterile CSF inflammation with pleocytosis or high protein, a severe-spectrum CAPS feature.
Raised intracranial pressure syndrome from chronic CNS inflammation.
Seizure burden from chronic or active CNS CAPS involvement.
Clinically apparent hearing impairment.
Progressive inner-ear inflammatory hearing loss, often high-frequency and partly irreversible after delay.
Average audiometric threshold elevation when hearing-loss severity is quantified.
Joint pain during inflammatory episodes.
Objective arthritis or joint swelling; may be episodic or chronic.
Muscle pain or limb heaviness during CAPS activity.
Patellar or knee bony overgrowth/hyperostosis from severe growth-plate involvement.
Craniofacial growth-plate phenotype seen in severe early-onset CAPS.
Persistently open anterior fontanelle as part of severe early-onset cranial skeletal involvement.
Digital clubbing associated with chronic severe NLRP3 inflammatory activity and growth-factor signaling.
Growth failure, poor weight gain, or chronic inflammatory undernutrition.
Abdominal pain can occur during CAPS inflammation but is not a defining axis.
Proteinuria from AA amyloid or kidney involvement.
Nephrotic syndrome due to renal AA amyloidosis.
Cumulative hazard of AA amyloid deposition under sustained SAA elevation.

axes.display_name: Permanent hearing loss hazard in CAPS
axes.clinical_meaning: Hazard that cochlear inflammation becomes irreversible.
Hazard of clinically important raised intracranial pressure from CNS inflammation.
Hazard of visual impairment from uveitis, optic-nerve involvement, or raised intracranial pressure.
Kidney-failure hazard downstream of AA amyloidosis or chronic renal damage.
Treatment-safety context for biologic immunomodulation.
Context for adjusting renally cleared therapies such as anakinra.
Access, cost, availability, or logistics limiting direct IL-1 blockade.
Adverse tolerance context that can reduce net benefit or require switching IL-1 blocker strategy.
Lifespan outcome hazard driven by severe CNS disease, infections under treatment, amyloidosis/kidney failure, neurologic complications, or irreversible organ damage.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Gain-of-function NLRP3 activity increases caspase-1 and IL-1 beta signaling.
NLRP3 dysregulation lowers the threshold for spontaneous or triggered flares.
IL-1 beta signaling recruits neutrophils and drives acute-phase systemic inflammation.
IL-1 beta-driven inflammation can involve ocular tissues and meninges.
Chronic cytokine activity inflames the inner ear and causes progressive hearing loss.
Musculoskeletal and growth-plate inflammation are downstream of the NLRP3/IL-1 pathway.
Persistent SAA elevation over time drives AA amyloid organ damage.
Recurrent sterile inflammatory episodes are the clinical expression of flare gating.
A recurrent CAPS history remains informative even when a current flare gate is not at peak intensity.
Severe CAPS may remain continuously inflamed between flares.
Cold exposure, physiologic stress, infection, vaccination, or exercise can trigger flares in part of the CAPS spectrum.
Trigger-sensitive episode history is a stable disease-pattern observation, not only a momentary flare state.
The flare gate determines the duration of each inflammatory episode.
More active disease produces more frequent attacks.
Neutrophilic skin inflammation produces rash.
The CAPS rash is commonly urticaria-like and evanescent.
Nonpruritic migratory morphology reflects neutrophilic pseudo-urticaria rather than histamine urticaria.
Panniculitis may occur in rare CAPS contexts but is not required.
IL-1 beta raises temperature during inflammatory activity.
Fever history captures recurrent attacks outside a single vital-sign snapshot.
Active CAPS raises acute-phase markers even when exact values are not reported.
CRP rises with CAPS inflammatory activity.
SAA rises with active inflammation and mediates amyloid risk.
ESR usually follows acute-phase protein elevation but may lag.
Sterile neutrophilic inflammation can produce marked leukocytosis.
Neutrophils dominate CAPS inflammatory response.
Reactive thrombocytosis can occur during sustained inflammation.
Chronic inflammation and nutritional effects can lower hemoglobin.
Conjunctivitis is a frequent ocular manifestation.
Uveitis occurs in more severe ocular involvement.
Papilledema reflects raised intracranial pressure or optic-nerve involvement.
Headache can accompany meningitis or intracranial hypertension.
Chronic aseptic meningitis is a severe CAPS manifestation.
Leptomeningeal inflammation can raise intracranial pressure.
Seizures can occur with chronic CNS inflammatory disease.
Cochlear inflammation produces clinically apparent hearing loss.
Inner-ear inflammation produces sensorineural loss.
Progressive cochlear inflammation raises audiometric thresholds.
Joint pain is common during inflammatory episodes.
Synovial and periarticular inflammation causes arthritis.
Myalgia can accompany CAPS flares.
Severe growth-plate involvement causes knee or patellar overgrowth.
Early severe disease can cause craniofacial skeletal changes.
Delayed fontanelle closure belongs to the severe cranial phenotype.
Clubbing can reflect chronic inflammatory growth-factor signaling.
Chronic systemic inflammation causes poor growth and weight gain.
Abdominal pain can occur in CAPS but should remain a non-defining supportive feature.
Renal AA amyloid commonly first appears as proteinuria.
Progressive renal amyloid can produce nephrotic syndrome.
Sustained SAA exposure raises AA amyloid hazard.
Delayed suppression of cochlear inflammation increases irreversible hearing loss risk.
CNS inflammation raises intracranial pressure hazard.
Papilledema, optic-nerve injury, or uveitis can threaten vision.
Renal amyloid can progress to kidney failure.
Severe CNS inflammation, seizures, raised intracranial pressure, and disability increase mortality risk.
AA amyloidosis and kidney failure are major late mortality drivers.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Rash and fever often occur together in active CAPS attacks.
Fever and CRP are both downstream of IL-1 activity.
CRP and SAA rise together as acute-phase reactants.
More recurrent disease tends to have more frequent attacks.
Triggered attacks often have coherent attack duration patterns.
Audiometry quantifies the severity of hearing loss.
Papilledema and intracranial hypertension are clinically linked.
Chronic articular inflammation and growth-plate overgrowth can co-occur.
Severe chronic inflammation can link poor growth and anemia.
Cumulative SAA exposure drives AA amyloid hazard.
Hearing loss mainly reduces function rather than directly causing death; hazard coupling is weak and indirect through severe-disease burden.
Severe intracranial hypertension and neurologic complications can increase mortality hazard.

treatments.clinical_role: Daily IL-1 receptor blockade that can rapidly suppress fever, rash, acute-phase markers, CNS inflammation, and SAA-driven damage risk when dose exposure is adequate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active serious infection complicates biologic immune suppression.
Renal impairment changes anakinra dosing and safety.
Treatment intolerance can limit daily injection therapy.

treatments.clinical_role: Long-acting IL-1 beta blockade for sustained suppression of systemic CAPS inflammation and acute-phase markers.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Long-acting IL-1 beta blockade is less flexible during uncontrolled infection.
Treatment intolerance can require switching agents or desensitization workflows.

treatments.clinical_role: Soluble IL-1 trap option for sustained control of milder to moderate CAPS inflammatory activity where available.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active serious infection lowers net biologic benefit.

treatments.display_name: IL-1 blockade dose optimization or switching
treatments.clinical_role: Adjusts dose, interval, adherence, or agent choice when residual inflammation, CNS disease, breakthrough flares, or access/tolerance context prevents adequate suppression.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Access constraints may force bridge therapy rather than adequate IL-1 blockade.

treatments.clinical_role: Temporary partial suppression of inflammatory symptoms while definitive cytokine-targeted access, diagnostics, or transition is arranged; it does not reliably prevent chronic organ damage alone.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Steroids can worsen uncontrolled infection and mask fever.

treatments.display_name: NSAID, antipyretic, and antihistamine symptom support
treatments.clinical_role: Symptom relief for fever, pain, or itch-mimic complaints; antihistamines often have little effect on neutrophilic CAPS rash and this strategy does not reshape the disease driver.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: NSAID exposure may be unsafe with kidney disease or amyloidosis.

treatments.clinical_role: Low-certainty resource-limited bridge or adjunct reported in selected cases when IL-1 blockade is unavailable; toxicity and incomplete organ protection must stay explicit.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: These agents appear mainly as alternatives when IL-1 blockade cannot be accessed.

treatments.clinical_role: Renal protection, proteinuria/nephrotic management, renal replacement planning, and transplant care when amyloidosis or CKD has emerged, paired with inflammation suppression.

treatments.display_name: Hearing, vision, and CNS rehabilitation and protection
treatments.clinical_role: Audiology, hearing aids or cochlear implantation, ophthalmology, intracranial-pressure management, seizure care, developmental support, and rehabilitation for established organ injury.

present.clinical_rationale: A pathogenic NLRP3 variant strongly supports the CAPS manifold, but case JSON should keep genetic confirmation non-ranking unless the workflow includes post-workup evidence.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Family history or de novo monogenic context supports recurrent sterile inflammation.
Early-onset chronic disease is more likely to affect growth.
Severe early disease can express skeletal growth effects.
Trigger-sensitive episodes are a real expression of part of the CAPS spectrum.
CNS/ocular phenotype raises papilledema and intracranial-risk expression.
Severe CNS involvement increases intracranial-pressure hazard.
Established hearing loss shifts the disease expression toward cochlear damage axes.
Existing hearing loss increases risk of irreversible damage.
Inadequate suppression permits persistent SAA elevation.
Renal amyloid context raises proteinuria expression.
Kidney failure is a major late mortality pathway.
Access constraints can leave inflammation active for longer.

treatment_effect_modulation.thalidomide_or_lenalidomide_resource_lim: context-specific bridge role becomes more relevant when IL-1 blockers cannot be accessed

supportive_care.clinical_role: Keep NLRP3 sequencing, final paper diagnosis, treatment response, and long-term outcome as confirmatory/non-ranking unless explicitly testing post-workup mode.
Trend CRP, SAA, CBC, urinalysis, urine protein, creatinine, and albumin to detect residual inflammation and AA amyloid risk.
Assess conjunctivitis, uveitis, papilledema, visual function, headache, raised intracranial pressure, CSF inflammation, seizures, and developmental effects.
Serial audiology is needed because high-frequency sensorineural loss may be subtle early and may become irreversible.
Monitor arthritis, knee/patellar overgrowth, frontal bossing, growth failure, gait, weight bearing, and physical function.
Because CAPS can mimic infection with fever, leukocytosis, and high CRP, evaluate serious infection while preserving the autoinflammatory vector; review vaccines, infection risk, and biologic safety.
Once diagnosis is established, use family history, genetic counseling, de novo/familial inheritance assessment, and reproductive counseling as clinical management context.

quality_notes: No clinical-ordering label fields are used.
The only derived_hazard axis is mortality_hazard_in_D-CAPS.
Disease-name scope remains pure: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome; internal spectrum features are represented structurally.
